summary.text: Take \(n=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where the two odd factors are prime. Rewriting the deficiency sum as \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\) and using multiplicativity across these coprime factors gives \(\sigma(n)=66183576284700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)=132367152569399\), hence \(a(n)=1\) although \(n\ne1,12\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e
\]
denote the sum of the positive divisors of the positive integer \(m\). The deficiency of \(m\) is
\[
\operatorname{def}(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
and the sequence in the conjecture is therefore
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will show that
\[
N=33\,085\,221\,781\,504
\]
is a counterexample: it is neither \(1\) nor \(12\), but \(a(N)=1\).

First rewrite the expression defining \(a(n)\). Put
\[
S(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Because \(\sum_{d\mid n}d=\sigma(n)\), we have the identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=\sum_{d\mid n}2d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-S(n). \tag{1}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus it suffices to evaluate \(\sigma(N)\) and \(S(N)\).

We use the factorization
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed,
\[
2^{14}=16384,\qquad 4409\cdot458009=2\,019\,361\,681,
\]
and multiplication gives
\[
16384\cdot2\,019\,361\,681=33\,085\,221\,781\,504.
\]
The numbers \(4409\) and \(458009\) are distinct odd primes. For completeness, their primality can be established by the following finite Lucas primality computation.

We use this elementary criterion: suppose the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known, and there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(r\mid m-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(m-1)/r}-1,m\bigr)=1. \tag{3}
\]
Then \(m\) is prime. To see why, let \(\ell\) be any prime divisor of \(m\). The first congruence shows that the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(\ell\) divides \(m-1\). If \(r^e\) is the exact power of a prime \(r\) dividing \(m-1\), condition (3) says that this order does not divide \((m-1)/r\), so the order must contain the full factor \(r^e\). This holds for every prime factor \(r\) of \(m-1\); hence the order is divisible by \(m-1\). It follows that the order is exactly \(m-1\). But an order modulo \(\ell\) is at most \(\ell-1\), so \(m-1\leq \ell-1\), or \(m\leq\ell\). Since \(\ell\mid m\), this forces \(\ell=m\), and therefore \(m\) is prime.

The following table gives recursive certificates using that criterion. In the last column, an entry \(r:c\) means
\[
b^{(m-1)/r}\equiv c\pmod m
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd(c-1,m)=1.
\]
For every row, direct repeated squaring also gives \(b^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
m & m-1 & b & r:c\\ \hline
3 & 2 & 2 & 2:2\\
5 & 2^2 & 2 & 2:4\\
7 & 2\cdot3 & 3 & 2:6,\;3:2\\
19 & 2\cdot3^2 & 2 & 2:18,\;3:7\\
29 & 2^2\cdot7 & 2 & 2:28,\;7:16\\
229 & 2^2\cdot3\cdot19 & 6 & 2:228,\;3:134,\;19:165\\
57251 & 2\cdot5^3\cdot229 & 2 & 2:57250,\;5:55371,\;229:48088\\
4409 & 2^3\cdot19\cdot29 & 3 & 2:4408,\;19:209,\;29:3965\\
458009 & 2^3\cdot57251 & 3 & 2:458008,\;57251:6561
\end{array}
\]

The displayed gcds are all \(1\), as a direct Euclidean-algorithm calculation shows. For example, in the last two rows the nontrivial checks are
\[
\gcd(208,4409)=\gcd(3964,4409)=1
\]
and
\[
\gcd(6560,458009)=1;
\]
the entries with residue \(m-1\) amount to \(\gcd(m-2,m)=1\) because all the displayed \(m\)'s are odd. The other listed gcds are similarly immediate finite Euclidean computations. Starting with the evident primality of \(2\), the rows successively prove the primality of every prime needed in the factorization of the next row’s \(m-1\). In particular, they prove that \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime.

Consequently, the three factors \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) in (2) are pairwise coprime. We may therefore use multiplicativity. Recall first that if \(x\) and \(y\) are coprime, every divisor of \(xy\) can be written uniquely as \(uv\), where \(u\mid x\) and \(v\mid y\), and \(u,v\) are themselves coprime. It follows that
\[
\sigma(xy)=\sigma(x)\sigma(y). \tag{4}
\]
The same divisor decomposition and (4) show that \(S\) is also multiplicative:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(xy)
 &=\sum_{d\mid xy}\sigma(d)\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}\sigma(uv)\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}\sigma(u)\sigma(v)\\
 &=S(x)S(y). \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]

We now evaluate these functions on the three factors of \(N\). The divisors of \(2^{14}\) are \(1,2,\ldots,2^{14}\), so
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767. \tag{6}
\]
Moreover, for \(0\leq j\leq14\),
\[
\sigma(2^j)=1+2+\cdots+2^j=2^{j+1}-1.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}\sigma(2^j)\\
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}(2^{j+1}-1)\\
 &=2\sum_{j=0}^{14}2^j-15\\
 &=2(2^{15}-1)-15\\
 &=65519. \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(p\) is prime, its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Therefore
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1
\]
and
\[
S(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2. \tag{8}
\]
Applying (8) to the two odd prime factors gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
p&\sigma(p)&S(p)\\ \hline
4409&4410&4411\\
458009&458010&458011.
\end{array} \tag{9}
\]

Using multiplicativity (4), together with (6) and (9), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\\
 &=144\,502\,470\cdot458010\\
 &=66\,183\,576\,284\,700. \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly, (5), (7), and (9) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(N)
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\\
 &=289\,004\,309\cdot458011\\
 &=132\,367\,152\,569\,399. \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting (10) and (11) into identity (1), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sigma(N)-S(N)\\
 &=2(66\,183\,576\,284\,700)
   -132\,367\,152\,569\,399\\
 &=132\,367\,152\,569\,400
   -132\,367\,152\,569\,399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally,
\[
N=33\,085\,221\,781\,504>12,
\]
so \(N\neq1\) and \(N\neq12\). Thus \(a(N)=1\) although \(N\) is neither of the two integers asserted by the conjecture. Therefore the statement
\[
\text{“for every positive integer }n,\quad a(n)=1
\iff n=1\text{ or }n=12\text{”}
\]
is false.
